desc:
You are given two integer arrays a and b of the same length n. You may rearrange the elements of a in any order you like (the order of b is fixed). After rearranging, the dot product is a[0]*b[0] + a[1]*b[1] + ... + a[n-1]*b[n-1].

Return the smallest dot product that can be obtained.

a = [1, 3, -5], b = [-2, 4, 1]   -> -25
(rearrange a to [1, -5, 3]... no: [3, 1, -5] with b gives -6 + 4 - 5 = -7; the best order is [-5, 3, 1]... )
hints: Try all orders for tiny arrays and look at which element of a ends up opposite which element of b.
To make the sum small you want large positive numbers multiplied by small (very negative) ones. Which of a's elements should face the largest element of b?
Sort a ascending and b descending and multiply element by element (the rearrangement inequality).
editorial: Suppose in some arrangement a[i] < a[j] but b[i] < b[j] as well. Then a[i]*b[i] + a[j]*b[j] is not smaller than a[i]*b[j] + a[j]*b[i], because the difference is (a[j]-a[i])*(b[j]-b[i]) ≥ 0. So swapping the two a-values never makes the product worse. Repeating until no such pair remains gives the arrangement where the order of a is the opposite of the order of b.
Implementation: sort a ascending, sort b descending, add up the products. That is O(n log n); the result is at most 5,000 × 10,000 in absolute value, well inside 32-bit range.
